5 homepage fixes local businesses should make first

A practical homepage checklist: clear offer, contact paths, mobile experience, trust signals, and one clear next step.

Published by NMark Designs · September 15, 2026 · 3 min read

In this guide

1. An offer that makes sense before scrolling2. One primary action, with no dead ends3. Mobile is a separate test, not a smaller desktop4. Build trust with evidence, not superlatives5. Make contact and local details accurate

Share this article

Send the article to someone who may find it useful.

FacebookLinkedInX

The short answer

A useful homepage answers five questions: what you offer, what to do next, whether it works on a phone, why to trust you and how to reach you. Check these before changing colours or adding animation.

1. An offer that makes sense before scrolling

Open the homepage and read only the heading and first sentence. Can you tell which service is offered and who it is for? If not, the problem is the message, not the size of the logo.

Imagine a local painting business. ‘Your vision, our passion’ says little about the work. ‘Interior painting and wall preparation’ provides immediate context. Add a service area only if it is accurate; do not insert city names just for keywords.

  • Name the main service in plain language.
  • Explain who it is for in one sentence.
  • Remove claims you cannot substantiate.

2. One primary action, with no dead ends

Choose an action that reflects how the business actually works: an enquiry, call or booking. A portfolio can be a secondary link without competing visually with contact.

‘Send an enquiry’ is more precise than ‘Learn more’ when the button opens a contact form. After clicking, visitors should get exactly what the label promises. Do not offer a free review unless you actually provide one.

  • Follow the main button on every important page.
  • Check that the form explains required fields and errors.
  • Repeat the same action label at the bottom of the page.

3. Mobile is a separate test, not a smaller desktop

Open the site on a real phone without zooming. A long headline, a menu covering content or a button squeezed against an edge can interrupt an enquiry. Test with a keyboard too: focus must remain visible.

A large photograph is not inherently a problem. Downloading an unnecessarily large file or shifting content as it loads is. Supply appropriate dimensions and reserve the image’s space in the layout.

  • Check text, navigation and contact on a narrow screen.
  • Do not hide essential information behind hover effects.
  • Test loading over a mobile connection too.

4. Build trust with evidence, not superlatives

Instead of ‘the best quality’, show relevant work and explain what was delivered. A project photograph with a little context is more useful than an anonymous compliment with no source.

Publish only approved references and verifiable information. Without measurements, describe decisions and scope rather than inventing sales growth. This helps readers and supports an accurate understanding of the page in search.

5. Make contact and local details accurate

The business name, phone number and service area should be consistent across the website and business profiles. An address is useful only when it is real and intended to be public. Do not invent a location for a service business without a public office.

Finally, ask someone unfamiliar with the site to find a service and send an agreed test enquiry. Note where they hesitate. Fix that obstacle and repeat the task: it is a more concrete next step than redesigning everything on instinct.
